subtopic_detail: HEEADSSS assessment - sensitive-topic phrasing with parent present
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a suburban general practice with her mother for a follow-up after 3 months of headaches, poor sleep and declining school marks. Her mother has done most of the talking so far and has stayed in the room. Basic history, examination and neurological assessment are unremarkable, and you have decided to complete a HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment before the visit ends.

When you gently signal a shift toward more personal questions, the mother says she would prefer to stay because "we do not have secrets". The girl looks at her feet and says nothing. There is no acute safety concern in the room and the appointment has time available.

data_table.Presentation: 3 months of headaches, poor sleep, declining marks
data_table.Examination: General and neurological examination within normal limits
data_table.Consultation dynamic: Mother has led the history; adolescent quiet and avoiding eye contact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to begin the HEEADSSS interview?

options.text: Explain that adolescent care works best when the young person is seen alone for part of the visit, invite the mother to the waiting room for the next ten minutes, and describe the limits of confidentiality before starting HEEADSSS
options.rationale: The RACGP and RCH adolescent frameworks recommend routinely offering time alone with the young person, normalising it as standard practice rather than singling this family out, and explicitly setting confidentiality limits (self-harm, harm to others, abuse) before sensitive questioning begins (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health; RCH CPG Engaging with and assessing the adolescent).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.text: Proceed with HEEADSSS in the mother's presence but soften the wording of every sensitive item so the adolescent is not embarrassed and can nod or shake her head instead of answering aloud in full sentences
options.rationale: Softening wording does not fix the core problem: a third party in the room will suppress disclosure about substances, sex, mood and abuse regardless of phrasing, and non-verbal answers cannot be safely interpreted (Source: RCH CPG; RACGP Adolescent Health).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.text: Defer HEEADSSS to a follow-up appointment booked without the mother in one week, and use today only for the physical complaint of headaches so the young person does not feel put on the spot in front of her parent
options.rationale: Deferring loses the opportunity today when a psychosocial driver is already suspected; time alone can be created now within the existing appointment and follow-up booked to consolidate (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health; RCH).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.text: Ask the mother directly what she believes is happening at home and at school first, using her account as the framework for HEEADSSS, then ask the adolescent to confirm or clarify each domain in her mother's presence
options.rationale: Parents provide useful collateral but the HEEADSSS is a first-person tool: adolescent-reported behaviours (substance use, sexuality, self-harm) are frequently unknown to the parent and will not surface if the parent frames the narrative (Source: RCH CPG; RACGP).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

options.text: Hand the adolescent a printed HEEADSSS questionnaire to complete silently in the room while you continue to speak with her mother about school performance and family stressors over the same ten-minute period
options.rationale: A written questionnaire in the parent's presence does not confer privacy (the parent can read it) and removes the clinician-led interview that identifies safety issues in real time (Source: RCH CPG; headspace clinical practice guidance).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

explanation.summary: HEEADSSS is a semi-structured psychosocial interview (Home, Education/Employment, Eating/Exercise, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety) that only works when the adolescent is interviewed alone with confidentiality limits made explicit up front. Australian adolescent-friendly practice normalises time alone as a routine part of every adolescent visit so no single family feels targeted, and frames confidentiality as bounded by mandatory-report triggers (self-harm risk, harm to others, abuse). Building this in from age 12-13 makes the transition easier at 14-16.
key_points: Offer time alone routinely, not just when a concern is suspected
State confidentiality limits before sensitive questioning: self-harm, harm to others, abuse
HEEADSSS domains: Home, Education, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide, Safety
Non-verbal answers and written forms in a parent's presence do not confer privacy
Collateral from parents is valuable but is added AFTER the adolescent-alone interview, not before
explanation.pearls: The three standard confidentiality-limit categories in RACGP/RCH adolescent practice are: intent to harm self, intent to harm others, and disclosed abuse. Naming them explicitly before HEEADSSS starts is protective for both parties. In context: adolescent psychosocial assessment fails without alone-time and explicit confidentiality limits, regardless of how carefully questions are worded (Source: RACGP; RCH).

sources.label: RCH CPG: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

subtopic_detail: CRAFFT screen interpretation and motivational interviewing entry point
stem:
A 16-year-old boy is reviewed alone in a regional headspace centre after his GP referred him for "partying too much". You have already explained the confidentiality limits and he has consented to a CRAFFT-based substance-use screen.

He reports drinking alcohol at parties on most weekends, occasional cannabis with friends, no other substances, no injecting drug use, and no acute intoxication today. He scores 3 on the CRAFFT (yes to Car, Forget, Friends; no to Relax, Alone, Trouble). Vital signs are within normal limits and his mental state is euthymic with no suicidal ideation. He tells you he does not think his use is a problem but is happy to keep talking.

data_table.Setting: 16-year-old male, alone, headspace consultation with confidentiality discussed
data_table.Substance history: Weekend alcohol, occasional cannabis, no other substances, no injecting
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no intoxication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to a residential adolescent alcohol and other drug rehabilitation unit for a structured 4-week withdrawal and relapse-prevention program including supervised abstinence and weekly urine drug screens
options.rationale: Residential rehabilitation is reserved for severe dependence, failed outpatient care, or unsafe home environment. A CRAFFT of 2+ warrants brief intervention, not automatic residential referral (Source: RACGP; headspace clinical practice guidance).

options.text: Commission a urine drug screen and full biochemistry today as the primary intervention, deferring any counselling or brief intervention until the objective substance results and liver function tests are back at the follow-up visit
options.rationale: Testing is not required for a self-disclosed adolescent substance history and delays the highest-yield intervention (brief MI at first contact). UDS may be adjunctive but is not the primary step (Source: headspace; RACGP).

options.text: Reassure him that weekend alcohol and occasional cannabis are normative for his age, take no further substance-related action today, and review only if he re-presents with a specific new alcohol or other drug related concern
options.rationale: Normalising a positive CRAFFT screen misses the intervention window; getting into a car with a substance-using driver (the C item) is itself a mortality-risk marker regardless of frequency (Source: CRAFFT 2.1 manual; RACGP).

options.text: Notify his parents of the CRAFFT results at the end of the visit without his consent because his substance use meets a threshold that overrides adolescent confidentiality under mandatory-reporting duties in this jurisdiction
options.rationale: Substance use in a competent adolescent without acute danger does not meet mandatory-report criteria; breaching confidentiality here would destroy the therapeutic alliance and is not required (Source: RACGP Adolescent health toolkit; NSW/Vic Children and Young Persons Act guidance).

options.text: Provide brief motivational interviewing today - explore importance and confidence to change, offer information on cannabis and alcohol harms, and agree a follow-up appointment within 2-4 weeks with brief-intervention documentation
options.rationale: A CRAFFT score of 2 or more identifies a young person at risk of a substance-use disorder and is an indication for brief intervention using motivational interviewing at the same visit. He is engaged and not intoxicated; the highest-yield step is a same-day MI conversation with structured follow-up (Source: RACGP; headspace; CRAFFT 2.1 manual).

explanation.summary: CRAFFT is the validated adolescent substance-use screen; a score of 2 or more identifies young people at risk of a substance-use disorder and prompts brief intervention rather than confirmatory testing or immediate residential referral. Motivational interviewing (explore importance/confidence, roll with resistance, elicit change talk) delivered at first contact has evidence for reducing harm even when the young person is not seeking treatment. Escalation to specialist AoD service is guided by dependence severity, mental-health comorbidity and social safety.
key_points: CRAFFT items: Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Friends, Trouble
CRAFFT >=2 = brief intervention indicated; CRAFFT >=4 = higher probability of DSM-5 SUD
MI at first contact is more effective than deferring to a follow-up visit
Confidentiality is not overridden by substance use alone in a competent adolescent
Escalate if dependence, injecting, polysubstance with sedatives, or psychiatric comorbidity
explanation.pearls: The C item (getting in a Car with a driver, including self, who is under the influence) is the strongest single mortality predictor of the CRAFFT items and is worth a direct safety plan on its own. In context: adolescent AoD screening is designed for brief intervention at the point of care, not for confirmatory laboratory workup (Source: CRAFFT 2.1; RACGP).

subtopic_detail: School refusal - anxiety-driven vs conduct-driven differentiation
stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought by her father to the GP because she has attended school on only 4 of the last 20 school days. On the mornings she stays home she complains of stomach aches and headaches, is tearful, and asks to be with her mother. She spends the day at home doing schoolwork online, does not seek out peers or games, and returns to bed. Weekends and school holidays are unremarkable.

She describes worry that "something bad will happen" to her mother if she is at school, denies being bullied, and denies substance use. There is no history of conduct problems, running away, or lying. Physical examination and basic bloods are within normal limits. Her father is exhausted and wants "a note keeping her home until she is ready".

data_table.Attendance: 4/20 school days over the last month
data_table.Somatic complaints: Morning stomach aches and headaches; resolve by afternoon
data_table.Behaviour at home: Stays in bed or does schoolwork; not with peers; no antisocial acts
data_table.Examination: Within normal limits; basic bloods within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Provide a medical certificate for extended home-based learning until the adolescent independently reports she feels ready to return, with GP review in 8 weeks and no active return-to-school plan in the interim
options.rationale: Sanctioning prolonged absence reinforces avoidance, which is the maintaining mechanism of anxiety-driven school refusal; the evidence-based approach is graded return with parent and school partnership (Source: RCH CPG School refusal; RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Refer to child protection services on grounds of educational neglect because school attendance has fallen below the state-mandated compulsory-attendance threshold and the father is not enforcing daily attendance at the school gate
options.rationale: The pattern is anxiety-driven school refusal (child stays with parent, no conduct features, symptom-free on weekends), not neglect or truancy; child protection is inappropriate here (Source: RCH CPG School refusal).

options.text: Formulate this as anxiety-driven school refusal and coordinate a graded return-to-school plan with parents and school welfare, refer for CBT-based psychology, and treat somatic complaints without further investigation
options.rationale: The clinical pattern (separation-themed worry, weekends symptom-free, no conduct features, family-based safety-seeking) is classic anxiety-driven school refusal. Evidence-based management is coordinated graded return with parent-school partnership, CBT-based psychology (including exposure), and validating rather than investigating somatic complaints (Source: RCH CPG School refusal; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily today as first-line intervention for presumed separation anxiety disorder, arrange fortnightly GP review for dose escalation to 50 mg, and defer psychological therapy until medication is titrated
options.rationale: SSRI treatment is second-line for adolescent anxiety after adequate CBT (with or without parent involvement); first-line is CBT and school engagement, not upfront pharmacotherapy (Source: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Undertake extensive gastrointestinal investigation including coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin, abdominal ultrasound and outpatient paediatric gastroenterology referral for recurrent abdominal pain before addressing school attendance
options.rationale: In the absence of red-flag features and with weekend-remitting somatic complaints, extensive GI workup is low-yield and delays the anxiety-focused intervention (Source: RCH CPG Chronic abdominal pain; RCH School refusal).

explanation.summary: School refusal splits along an anxiety vs conduct axis. Anxiety-driven refusal presents with distress at separation, somatic complaints that remit on weekends and holidays, staying at or near home rather than seeking peers, and no antisocial behaviour. Conduct-driven truancy presents with peer-group activity away from home, no distress on non-attendance, and often lying or rule-breaking. Anxiety-driven refusal responds to graded exposure via a return-to-school plan plus CBT; certificates sanctioning absence and pharmacotherapy-first approaches worsen outcomes.
key_points: Anxiety-driven pattern: distress + somatic + weekends OK + stays home + no conduct
Conduct-driven pattern: no distress + peer-directed absence + antisocial features
Graded return-to-school plan is first-line, not extended absence
CBT with parent involvement is first-line therapy; SSRI is second-line
Extensive somatic workup without red flags reinforces the illness model
explanation.pearls: The weekend-remitting somatic pattern is the single most useful discriminator: true GI or headache pathology does not politely disappear at 3 pm on Friday. In context: adolescent school refusal is treated by re-exposing the child to school in graded steps, not by removing the exposure (Source: RCH; RANZCP FCAP).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Cyberbullying with self-harm ideation - safety planning priority
stem:
A 14-year-old girl is seen alone in a headspace outreach clinic after her school counsellor referred her. Over 6 weeks a group of former friends have posted altered images of her on a public social-media account and sent group-chat messages calling her worthless. She has become withdrawn, sleeps 4-5 hours, and marks have fallen.

Today she discloses that on two occasions in the past week she has thought "it would be easier not to be here" while lying in bed at night, but has no plan, has not accessed means, and finds the thoughts frightening. She has never self-harmed. She has a supportive mother who is aware of some but not all of the online content and lives in the family home. Vital signs are within normal limits and she has consented to your involvement of her mother.

data_table.Cyberbullying: 6 weeks; altered images publicly posted; group-chat harassment
data_table.Suicidality: Passive ideation twice in past week; no plan, no means, no prior self-harm; ideation is ego-dystonic
data_table.Family: Supportive mother, lives at home; adolescent consents to mother involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Complete a collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping strategies and adult supports, engage her mother today, report the material to the eSafety Commissioner and the platform, and arrange psychology review within 1 week
options.rationale: Passive ideation without plan/means/self-harm history is managed with a same-visit collaborative safety plan (Stanley-Brown-style), adult support activation and early follow-up, not inpatient admission. Cyberbullying image-based abuse of a minor is reportable to the eSafety Commissioner, which can compel takedown under the Online Safety Act 2021 (Source: headspace CPG; eSafety Commissioner; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Arrange same-day involuntary transfer to a paediatric emergency department under the Mental Health Act for assessment and consideration of admission to an adolescent psychiatric inpatient unit for suicide risk observation
options.rationale: Passive ideation without plan, means or prior self-harm does not meet involuntary criteria; unnecessary admission fragments school and family supports and disrupts the therapeutic frame (Source: headspace CPG; state Mental Health Act guidance).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily today as first-line pharmacotherapy for presumed adolescent major depression, arrange GP review in 2 weeks for dose review, and defer psychological therapy until the SSRI has had time to work
options.rationale: She may develop depression but a formal MDD diagnosis and staged treatment plan cannot be justified today; SSRIs also carry a black-box early-treatment suicidality warning that mandates baseline safety planning and monitoring regardless (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; headspace CPG).

options.text: Reassure her that ignoring the messages, blocking the accounts and giving the situation time is the most effective strategy, without any external reporting or safety plan today, and review at the next scheduled headspace visit
options.rationale: Passive ignoring alone does not address image-based abuse, and no safety plan is documented; a passive ideation disclosure requires a same-visit response (Source: headspace CPG; eSafety Commissioner).

options.text: Advise the mother to contact the parents of the alleged perpetrators directly to seek an apology and voluntary removal of the material, and defer any professional or regulatory reporting until that private approach has been attempted
options.rationale: Peer-to-parent negotiation is not required before eSafety reporting, can escalate the situation, and delays image takedown; the Online Safety Act provides a rapid formal pathway (Source: eSafety Commissioner).

explanation.summary: Adolescent cyberbullying with passive suicidal ideation is managed at the level of the ideation, not the substrate: passive ideation without plan or means is safety-planned in the community with adult supports and early follow-up. Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 empowers the eSafety Commissioner to require rapid removal of cyberbullying material targeting a minor and image-based abuse; formal reporting is both a therapeutic and a protective act. SSRI treatment is not first-line at this presentation stage and requires established depression plus stepped-care rationale.
key_points: Passive ideation, no plan, no means, no history = community safety plan, not admission
eSafety Commissioner can compel takedown of cyberbullying targeting a minor
Involve a trusted adult with the young person's consent wherever possible
SSRI early treatment carries black-box suicidality monitoring requirements
Escalate to ED only if plan, means, prior serious self-harm, or acute intoxication
explanation.pearls: The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention has 6 steps: warning signs, internal coping, social distractions, adults who can help, professionals + crisis lines, means restriction. In context: adolescent suicide risk stratification determines the level of care, and cyberbullying requires a parallel regulatory response via eSafety (Source: headspace; eSafety).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

subtopic_detail: Conduct disorder vs oppositional defiant disorder - pathway to antisocial personality disorder
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought by his mother to the GP after being suspended from school for the third time this year. Over 18 months he has repeatedly bullied a smaller classmate, damaged a neighbour's fence, been caught shoplifting from a supermarket twice, and been aggressive to a family dog. He has been out overnight without telling his mother on two occasions in the past 3 months and has been truant from school on more than 20 days.

He shows no remorse when asked directly. He denies substance use and hallucinations, and mental state is otherwise unremarkable with normal affect and no psychotic features. There is no head injury history. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Behaviours (18 months): Bullying, property destruction, shoplifting x2, cruelty to animals, truancy >20 days, running away x2
data_table.Mental state: No remorse, no psychosis, no depressive features, no substance use
data_table.Medical: No head injury; vital signs within normal limits

lead_in: Which of the following best characterises this presentation and its long-term risk?

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder with a low probability of progression, best managed with parent management training and school-based behavioural supports and unlikely to require any specialist mental-health follow-up beyond adolescence
options.rationale: ODD is limited to defiance, argumentativeness and vindictiveness towards authority; the presence of aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit/theft and serious rule violation over 12 months meets DSM-5 conduct disorder, not ODD (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Early-onset schizophreniform disorder with negative symptoms, requiring urgent referral to the early intervention psychosis service for ultra-high-risk assessment and consideration of low-dose atypical antipsychotic pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: There are no positive symptoms, no attenuated psychotic symptoms, no functional decline of the ultra-high-risk pattern, and mental state is otherwise normal; conduct behaviours are not negative symptoms (Source: EPPIC EIS clinical practice guidance).

options.text: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder combined presentation with untreated comorbid learning disorder, best managed by trial of methylphenidate immediate release and educational assessment for a formal learning-support plan at school
options.rationale: There are no core inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms described and no learning-disorder features; the behaviour cluster is rule-violating not attention-based (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Adolescent-onset conduct disorder with limited pro-social emotions specifier, associated with substantially increased risk of adult antisocial personality disorder, warranting parent management training and multi-systemic therapy referral
options.rationale: The 4 DSM-5 conduct-disorder criteria groups (aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit/theft, serious rule violation) are met over 12 months. Absence of remorse meets the limited prosocial emotions specifier, which predicts higher risk of adult antisocial personality disorder. Evidence-based treatments are parent management training and multi-systemic therapy, not medication (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG158).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG158 Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder with paediatric-onset criteria met early, warranting immediate diagnostic disclosure, personality-focused psychotherapy referral, and documentation of the personality-disorder diagnosis in the medical record
options.rationale: Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18 by DSM-5-TR criteria (though a history of conduct disorder before 15 is required); paediatric labelling of a personality disorder is inappropriate (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is defined by a persistent pattern (>=3 criteria over 12 months) across four groups: aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceit or theft, and serious violations of rules. ODD is a narrower defiance/argumentativeness/vindictiveness pattern without the aggression, destruction and theft. The DSM-5 limited prosocial emotions specifier (lack of remorse, callousness, shallow affect, unconcern about performance) marks a group with higher progression to adult antisocial personality disorder. Evidence-based treatments for conduct disorder are behavioural family interventions and multi-systemic therapy; pharmacotherapy is limited to comorbid ADHD or targeted aggression.
key_points: CD requires >=3 criteria over 12 months across 4 groups
ODD = defiance without aggression/destruction/theft
Limited prosocial emotions specifier predicts adult ASPD risk
Parent management training and MST are first-line
ASPD is not diagnosed before age 18
explanation.pearls: Cruelty to animals is one of the DSM-5 conduct-disorder Group 1 criteria (aggression to people or animals) and is a specific antisocial-trajectory marker rather than an ADHD or ODD sign. In context: adolescent externalising presentations must be sub-typed accurately because the treatment (behavioural family therapy vs medication) and long-term prognosis differ substantially (Source: DSM-5-TR; NICE NG158).

sources.label: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG158 Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders

subtopic_detail: ARFID vs picky eating - thresholds for concern
stem:
A 13-year-old boy is brought to a paediatric outpatient clinic because he eats only 6 foods (white bread, plain pasta, chicken nuggets, apples, cheese, and milk) and refuses all others due to texture and smell. This pattern has been present since age 4 and has narrowed further in the past year.

He is on the 3rd centile for weight, has fallen from the 25th to the 3rd centile over 2 years, is fatigued, and has iron deficiency (ferritin 6 micrograms/L, reference 20-300) with mild microcytic anaemia. There is no fear of weight gain, no body-image distress, no purging, no exercise-driving, and he wants to eat more variety but cannot tolerate it. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Diet: 6-food repertoire since age 4, narrowing further; texture/smell-driven
data_table.Growth: Weight 3rd centile; fallen from 25th centile over 2 years
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 6 micrograms/L (20-300), microcytic anaemia; UEC/LFT within normal limits
data_table.Psychopathology: No fear of weight gain, no body-image distress, no purging, no compulsive exercise

lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atypical anorexia nervosa presenting with fear of texture rather than weight, with a similar treatment pathway and prognosis and requiring family-based therapy directed at weight restoration and reintroduction of feared foods
options.rationale: Anorexia nervosa and its atypical form require fear of weight gain or body-image disturbance; a texture-driven restriction without weight concern is ARFID, not AN (Source: DSM-5-TR; ANZAED).

options.text: Longstanding picky eating within normal developmental variation, with no specific mental-health intervention needed beyond parental reassurance, gradual exposure at family meals, and routine child-health surveillance at annual checks
options.rationale: Picky eating in typical variants does not cross the failure-to-grow or nutritional-deficiency threshold; falling from 25th to 3rd centile with iron deficiency crosses into diagnosable ARFID (Source: DSM-5-TR; RCH).

options.text: Avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder driven by sensory sensitivity, meeting DSM-5 criteria via faltering growth and nutritional deficiency, requiring a multidisciplinary eating disorder pathway including dietitian and psychology
options.rationale: ARFID is diagnosed when restriction (sensory, low interest, or aversive experience) produces one or more of: significant weight loss/failure to gain, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements/enteral feeds, or psychosocial impairment - WITHOUT fear of weight gain or body-image distortion. This presentation meets both weight-trajectory and deficiency criteria and requires MDT care (Source: DSM-5-TR; ANZAED; RCH).

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder with associated food selectivity, best managed by autism-specific behavioural intervention alone without formal eating-disorder pathway involvement, and referral to a developmental paediatrician as the primary service
options.rationale: Sensory food selectivity is common in ASD and can co-occur with ARFID, but a growth-failure and nutritional-deficiency pattern meets the ARFID threshold in its own right and needs eating-disorder-specific input alongside any ASD assessment (Source: DSM-5-TR; ANZAED).

options.text: Coeliac disease with secondary food avoidance from post-prandial symptoms, requiring urgent coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy before any psychological or dietetic diagnosis is considered, and gluten-free trial deferred until confirmed
options.rationale: Coeliac serology is reasonable to exclude organic causes but does not explain the texture-driven 6-food repertoire since age 4; ARFID is a positive diagnosis, not a diagnosis of exclusion (Source: DSM-5-TR; GESA).

explanation.summary: ARFID sits between picky eating (no functional impairment) and anorexia nervosa (fear of weight gain, body-image distortion). DSM-5 requires that restriction produces one of: significant weight loss/failure to grow, nutritional deficiency, dependence on enteral feeds/oral supplements, or marked psychosocial interference - WITHOUT the AN cognitive features. The three ARFID subtypes are sensory sensitivity, low interest in eating, and post-traumatic aversive presentation. AU management is multidisciplinary (paediatrician, dietitian, psychology) with age-appropriate feeding therapy and comorbidity (ASD, anxiety) screening.
key_points: ARFID = restriction with impairment WITHOUT AN cognitive features
Any one of weight loss/deficiency/supplement dependence/psychosocial interference qualifies
3 subtypes: sensory, low interest, post-traumatic aversive
Co-occurs with ASD, ADHD and anxiety disorders
AU pathway: paediatrician + dietitian + eating-disorder psychology
explanation.pearls: In ARFID a full paediatric eating-disorder assessment includes ferritin, vitamin D, B12, folate, zinc and a resting ECG (long QT risk with severe restriction and refeeding). In context: adolescent restrictive-eating presentations must be sub-typed accurately because ARFID and AN diverge in aetiology, therapy content and family-therapy approach (Source: ANZAED; RCH).

subtopic_detail: Adolescent major depression - first-line SSRI and monitoring
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a Melbourne GP with her mother, referred by the school counsellor for 4 months of low mood, anhedonia, initial insomnia, poor concentration, and marked functional decline. She meets DSM-5 criteria for a moderate-to-severe major depressive episode. She has had 10 sessions of individual CBT over 3 months at headspace with a certified therapist without meaningful benefit and the therapist has recommended stepping up.

She denies psychotic symptoms, denies past mania or hypomania, and denies substance use. She has current passive suicidal ideation with no plan or means; she has agreed to a safety plan and her mother has consented to involvement and means restriction. Weight, growth, LFTs, TSH and glucose are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder.

data_table.Prior treatment: 10 sessions CBT at headspace with recommendation to step up
data_table.Suicidality: Passive ideation, no plan/means, safety plan documented, means restricted
data_table.Bipolar screen: Negative personal and family history; no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Weight/growth, TSH, LFTs, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily as first-line SSRI for adolescent depression, continue CBT concurrently, and review at 1 week for tolerability and emergent suicidality per the black-box early-treatment warning
options.rationale: Sertraline is a reasonable SSRI in some contexts, but fluoxetine is the only SSRI with a TGA-approved paediatric depression indication in Australia and the strongest RCT evidence base for adolescent MDD (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 15 mg orally at night as first-line antidepressant to address depressive insomnia and poor appetite, continue CBT concurrently, and review at 2 weeks for weight, sedation and mood response
options.rationale: Mirtazapine lacks adolescent-specific efficacy evidence for major depression and is not first-line; using its sedative side-effect profile as the prescribing rationale is a common error (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg orally daily as first-line antidepressant, arrange fortnightly review for tolerability, and continue CBT concurrently while dose is escalated to a target of 75 to 150 mg daily
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has a poor benefit-risk balance in adolescent depression (increased suicidality signal without efficacy advantage over SSRIs) and is not first-line for this age group (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily as first-line, continue CBT concurrently, and review at 1 week then 2-weekly for the first 4 weeks for tolerability and emergent suicidality per the black-box early-treatment warning
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the SSRI with a TGA-approved paediatric depression indication and the largest evidence base (TADS trial). It is combined with continued CBT for best outcomes and requires close early-treatment monitoring (weekly for 4 weeks then 2-weekly) for the well-documented paediatric emergent suicidality signal (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Continue CBT alone for a further 8 weeks at higher intensity without any pharmacological step-up because SSRIs in adolescents carry unacceptable early-treatment suicidality risk that outweighs the potential efficacy benefit at any dose
options.rationale: CBT alone has already failed at adequate dose; combined SSRI + CBT is more effective than either alone for moderate-severe adolescent MDD. The black-box warning mandates monitoring, not avoidance (Source: RANZCP FCAP; TG Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for adolescent moderate-to-severe major depression in Australia is fluoxetine, the only SSRI with a TGA paediatric depression indication and the strongest RCT evidence (TADS: combined fluoxetine + CBT superior to either alone). Sertraline and escitalopram are reasonable second-line SSRIs. Venlafaxine is avoided (worse risk profile). Every SSRI initiation in a person under 25 carries a black-box early-treatment emergent-suicidality warning: weekly review for 4 weeks then 2-weekly, with a safety plan and means restriction in place. Bipolar screen must be negative before SSRI initiation.
key_points: Fluoxetine is first-line adolescent SSRI in Australia (TGA-approved)
Combined SSRI + CBT beats either alone for moderate-severe MDD
Screen for bipolar before starting any antidepressant
Weekly monitoring x 4 weeks, then 2-weekly, for emergent suicidality
Safety plan + means restriction documented before script
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine's long half-life (72 h for norfluoxetine metabolite) makes it more forgiving of missed doses and less prone to discontinuation syndrome, which suits adolescent adherence patterns. In context: adolescent depression pharmacotherapy is a stepped decision after adequate psychological therapy trial, not a first-visit reflex (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RANZCP FCAP).

subtopic_detail: NSSI vs suicide attempt - function and DBT-A indication
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is seen in a community mental-health clinic after her mother found superficial linear cuts on her forearms. Over the past 8 months she has cut herself with a pencil sharpener blade 2-3 times per week, always superficially, only when overwhelmed by strong emotions (anger, shame after arguments with her mother), and the cutting reliably reduces the intensity of the feeling within minutes.

She does not want to die and has never intended to die when cutting. She has no plan or intent for suicide today and denies past suicide attempts. She has emotion-regulation difficulties, an unstable sense of self, and chronic emptiness. There is a strong family history of anxiety. Vital signs are within normal limits and cuts are superficial with no deep-tissue involvement.

data_table.Self-harm pattern: 8 months, 2-3 x/week, superficial cuts to forearms, emotion-regulation function
data_table.Suicidal intent: Absent, both historically and today; no past attempts
data_table.Personality features: Emotion dysregulation, unstable self, chronic emptiness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management pathway?

options.text: Categorise this as suicidal behaviour and arrange same-day admission to an adolescent inpatient unit under the Mental Health Act with 24-hour observation, means restriction, and structured risk assessment on discharge planning
options.rationale: This is non-suicidal self-injury (emotion-regulation function, no intent to die, superficial pattern) not a suicide attempt; involuntary admission mislabels the behaviour and iatrogenically reinforces it in some presentations (Source: RANZCP FCAP; headspace CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Reassure her that self-harm without suicidal intent carries no long-term risk and does not require psychological therapy beyond routine GP mental-health care, and provide sterile dressings and general wound-care advice today
options.rationale: NSSI without suicidal intent nonetheless increases prospective risk of future suicide attempt and warrants targeted therapy; wound-care alone is inadequate (Source: RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG225 Self-harm).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG225 Self-harm assessment and management

options.text: Formulate as non-suicidal self-injury with emerging borderline traits, refer for adolescent-modified dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT-A), and support the family with skills coaching alongside a documented individual safety plan
options.rationale: The behaviour is NSSI (emotion-regulation function, no intent to die, superficial repetitive pattern) in a young person with emerging borderline features. DBT-A (16-24 weeks, individual + skills + family + phone coaching) has the strongest RCT evidence for reducing NSSI and suicidal behaviour in adolescents with these features (Source: RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG225; Miller DBT-A manual).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG225 Self-harm assessment and management

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg orally at night as first-line pharmacological treatment for emotion dysregulation and superficial self-harm, with review in 4 weeks for sedation, weight change and reduction in cutting frequency
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for NSSI or adolescent emerging BPD; psychological therapy (DBT-A) is; medication is adjunctive for specific comorbidities like depression or PTSD (Source: RANZCP FCAP; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Refer for standard supportive counselling only, avoid any specific structured therapy, and defer a personality-focused formulation until age 18 in case a formal borderline personality disorder diagnosis becomes clinically appropriate
options.rationale: Emerging BPD features in adolescents can and should be formulated and treated in adolescence; deferring evidence-based DBT-A to adulthood loses the developmental treatment window (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Chanen Chartsheet).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: NSSI (non-suicidal self-injury) is distinguished from a suicide attempt by function (emotion regulation, communication, self-punishment) and by absence of intent to die. Australian and international guidelines (RANZCP FCAP, NICE NG225) treat NSSI in adolescents with emerging BPD features using adolescent-modified DBT (Miller, Rathus and Linehan), which combines individual therapy, multi-family skills groups, phone coaching and therapist consultation over 16-24 weeks. NSSI nonetheless raises prospective suicide risk and demands a safety plan and family support. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive for specific comorbidities.
key_points: NSSI: no intent to die, function is affect-regulation/communication/self-punishment
NSSI still raises prospective suicide risk despite different intent
DBT-A is the highest-evidence therapy for adolescent NSSI + emerging BPD
Emerging BPD can and should be formulated in adolescence (Chanen et al)
Meds are adjunctive: SSRI for depression, no antipsychotic first-line for NSSI
explanation.pearls: Adolescent-modified DBT (DBT-A) includes a multi-family skills group and a fifth 'walking the middle path' skills module addressing dialectical family conflicts, which is not present in adult DBT. In context: adolescent self-harm must be sub-typed by function and intent because that determines whether the pathway is DBT-A, MDD treatment, or emergency risk management (Source: RANZCP FCAP; NICE NG225).

subtopic_detail: Gillick / Mature Minor mental-health consent + confidentiality limits
stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a Sydney general practice alone. She has 3 months of low mood, initial insomnia and anhedonia meeting criteria for a moderate major depressive episode, has completed 8 sessions of CBT at headspace without benefit, and after informed discussion wants to start fluoxetine.

She demonstrates understanding of the diagnosis, the black-box early-treatment suicidality warning, the need for weekly monitoring, potential sexual side effects and discontinuation issues, and she can explain her reasoning coherently. She lives with both parents. Her mother knows she has been at headspace but has not been told about today's visit; the young person is worried her father would react badly and asks that neither parent be informed today. There is passive suicidal ideation without plan or means and she has agreed to a safety plan. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Diagnosis and prior care: Moderate MDD; 8 sessions CBT without benefit
data_table.Capacity assessment: Understands diagnosis, risks/benefits, monitoring, alternatives; coherent reasoning
data_table.Family: Lives with both parents; mother partially informed; adolescent requests no disclosure today
data_table.Safety: Passive ideation, no plan/means, safety plan agreed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding consent and confidentiality?

options.text: Decline to prescribe today on the basis that a mental-health medication in an adolescent requires written parental consent in New South Wales, regardless of the young person's demonstrated capacity to consent to her own treatment
options.rationale: NSW does not impose a blanket age or parental-consent rule; a mature minor with capacity can consent to her own treatment under the Gillick / mature minor doctrine adopted in Australia (Marion's Case, HCA 1992) (Source: RACGP Adolescent Health; AHPRA/Medical Board of Australia).

options.text: Prescribe today on her demonstrated mature-minor capacity, document the capacity assessment and confidentiality limits, and encourage but do not compel parental disclosure with review at next visit
options.rationale: Gillick / mature minor competence (adopted in Australia via Marion's Case) permits a capable adolescent to consent to her own treatment. The clinician's task is to (a) formally assess and document capacity, (b) explain the fixed confidentiality limits (self-harm, harm to others, abuse), (c) actively encourage - but not compel - parental involvement, and (d) reassess at each visit (Source: RACGP; RANZCP FCAP; NSW Health youth consent guidance).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Telephone the mother today without the adolescent's consent because SSRI initiation in a minor overrides the confidentiality expectation and requires parental awareness of the black-box early-treatment suicidality warning at all times
options.rationale: A capable minor's consent is not overridden by the existence of a black-box warning; unilateral parental disclosure without a mandatory-report trigger breaches confidentiality and the therapeutic frame (Source: RACGP; AHPRA).

options.text: Refer directly to the child and adolescent mental health service (CAMHS) and refuse to prescribe fluoxetine in general practice for anyone under 16 in New South Wales because of local-jurisdictional prescribing restrictions on adolescent SSRI use
options.rationale: There is no such NSW prescribing restriction; GPs can and do initiate fluoxetine in capable adolescents after inadequate psychological therapy trial (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; RACGP).

options.text: Provide a limited script for one week only and use the constraint to compel the adolescent to bring a parent to the next visit for continuation, framing it as a safety-monitoring requirement rather than as a confidentiality override
options.rationale: Using medication supply as coercion to force parental disclosure breaches consent principles and is not the correct mechanism to encourage parental involvement (Source: AHPRA; RACGP).

explanation.summary: The Gillick or mature minor doctrine (established in the UK, adopted in Australia by the High Court in Marion's Case, 1992) recognises that a young person under 18 with sufficient understanding and intelligence can consent to their own medical treatment. Australian jurisdictions do not impose a blanket age below which parental consent is required for a competent minor's own care. The clinician's duties are: assess and document capacity for the specific decision, explain the fixed confidentiality limits (harm to self, harm to others, disclosure of abuse), actively encourage parental involvement without compelling it, and reassess at every visit. Special protections apply to certain interventions such as gender-affirming care and sterilisation.
key_points: Australia recognises Gillick / mature minor competence via Marion's Case (HCA 1992)
Capacity is decision-specific, not global; reassess each visit
Confidentiality limits: harm to self, harm to others, abuse disclosure
Encourage parental involvement; do not compel unless a limit is met
Coercing disclosure through prescription limits is a breach, not a workaround
explanation.pearls: The four documentation elements of a mature-minor consent are: understanding of the condition, understanding of the proposed treatment (benefits and risks), understanding of alternatives (including no treatment), and ability to weigh and communicate a decision. In context: adolescent mental-health prescribing is legally and ethically permissible in a capable minor, and clinicians who default to parental consent overstep in the other direction (Source: RACGP; AHPRA).

subtopic_detail: Anorexia MARSIPAN-AU admission criteria and refeeding risk
stem:
A 15-year-old girl is reviewed in an emergency department after her GP referred her with restrictive eating and rapid weight loss over 4 months. She weighs 38 kg (height 165 cm, BMI 14.0), has lost 18 percent of her body weight, and has been drinking water only for the last 48 hours.

Seated pulse rate is 38/min, supine BP 88/54 with a postural drop to 68/40, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 percent, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius. Investigations: potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), magnesium 0.65 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 490 ms. She denies suicidal ideation, has a supportive family, and wants to get better.

data_table.Anthropometry: 38 kg, 165 cm, BMI 14.0; 18% weight loss over 4 months
data_table.Vital signs: PR 38, supine BP 88/54, postural drop to 68/40, RR 16, SpO2 98%, T 35.4°C
data_table.Biochemistry: K 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5); Mg 0.65 mmol/L (0.7-1.0); glucose 3.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with same-day dietitian and family-based treatment referral, arrange GP review in 48 hours for repeat electrolytes, and agree an outpatient meal plan targeting slow weight gain and progressive oral refeeding
options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk criteria are met (bradycardia <40, postural hypotension with 20 mmHg systolic drop, hypokalaemia, QTc >450 ms, hypothermia); outpatient management would be unsafe (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

options.text: Admit to a paediatric medical ward for cardiac monitoring, cautious refeeding under MARSIPAN-AU with electrolyte replacement and thiamine before caloric load, and involve the specialist eating-disorder service from day 1
options.rationale: MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk features (bradycardia <40, postural drop >=20 systolic, K <3.0, QTc >450, hypothermia, phosphate low) mandate medical admission for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding. First 48-72 h prioritises electrolyte replacement (K, PO4, Mg) and thiamine BEFORE full caloric load to prevent refeeding syndrome; specialist ED input from day 1 (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020; RCH CPG Eating disorders).

options.text: Transfer to an adolescent psychiatric unit for weight restoration and family-based treatment initiation because her medical status is stable enough for a purely psychiatric admission and behavioural containment is the priority
options.rationale: She has multiple MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk medical features; a psychiatric unit does not have cardiac monitoring or the refeeding syndrome resources. Medical stabilisation precedes psychiatric admission (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

options.text: Commence high-caloric nasogastric refeeding at 2000 kcal/day from day 1 in the emergency department to correct starvation rapidly and reduce the length of the medical admission and total inpatient stay for the family
options.rationale: Rapid high-caloric refeeding in this biochemistry precipitates refeeding syndrome (further phosphate drop, cardiac failure, Wernicke). MARSIPAN-AU starts cautiously (~20 kcal/kg/day) with pre-emptive electrolyte and thiamine replacement (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg intravenous crystalloid bolus for postural hypotension and reassess disposition in 4 hours based on repeat vital signs before deciding whether medical admission or outpatient management is more appropriate
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid bolus in refeeding-vulnerable anorexia risks precipitating cardiac failure and worsening electrolyte disturbance; the disposition is already determined by MARSIPAN-AU criteria (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020).

explanation.summary: MARSIPAN-AU (Australian adaptation of the UK MARSIPAN framework) stratifies anorexia nervosa medical risk by anthropometric, cardiovascular, biochemical and behavioural criteria. Very-high-risk features (BMI <13 or <70% median for age, HR <40, systolic BP postural drop >=20 mmHg, K <3.0, PO4 <0.5, QTc >450 ms, temperature <35.5) mandate medical admission for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding. Refeeding syndrome (further drops in phosphate, potassium, magnesium, plus thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke's) is the main early risk; therefore start low-calorie (~20 kcal/kg/day) with pre-emptive electrolyte + thiamine, monitor daily, and titrate up. Family-based treatment (FBT) is the outpatient framework after medical stabilisation.
key_points: MARSIPAN-AU very-high-risk = medical admission, not outpatient or psych ward
HR <40, postural systolic drop >=20 mmHg, K <3.0, QTc >450 all trigger admission
Refeeding syndrome: PO4/K/Mg drop, thiamine deficiency, cardiac failure
Start ~20 kcal/kg/day; replace electrolytes and thiamine BEFORE caloric escalation
FBT (Maudsley) is the first-line outpatient therapy for adolescent AN post-stabilisation
explanation.pearls: The QTc >450 ms threshold in MARSIPAN-AU is more conservative than the general cardiology 470/480 cut-off because malnutrition adds electrolyte and cardiac muscle vulnerability. In context: adolescent AN medical management is governed by MARSIPAN-AU, not by BMI alone, and refeeding is always cautious and monitored (Source: ANZAED MARSIPAN-AU 2020; RCH).

subtopic_detail: Bulimia nervosa - FBT-BN vs CBT-E choice in an adolescent
stem:
A 16-year-old girl attends an eating-disorder outpatient clinic after a headspace referral. Over 6 months she has had 3-4 objective binge episodes per week followed by self-induced vomiting, with intense guilt and shape/weight over-evaluation. Her weight is on the 50th centile.

Biochemistry, ECG and dental review are within normal limits and she is medically stable. She lives at home with two engaged parents who want to be involved in her treatment, has no comorbid substance use, no active suicidal ideation, and no history of childhood trauma that would preclude family-based work. She has never had structured eating-disorder therapy. She has consented to family involvement in whatever plan is chosen and is motivated to change.

data_table.Diagnosis: Bulimia nervosa; 3-4 binge/purge episodes weekly for 6 months
data_table.Weight and medical: 50th centile; biochemistry, ECG, dental review within normal limits
data_table.Family: Two engaged parents, consenting to involvement, no trauma contraindication
data_table.Comorbidity: No substance use; no active suicidality; no prior structured ED therapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line psychological therapy?

options.text: Family-based treatment for bulimia (FBT-BN) as first-line, with the family taking initial control of eating and interruption of binge and purge cycles, transitioning to adolescent autonomy in phases 2 and 3
options.rationale: In adolescents with bulimia nervosa where family is engaged and there is no contraindication (severe trauma, parental psychopathology preventing engagement), FBT-BN is first-line in Australian guidance and has RCT evidence for higher abstinence rates at end of treatment than individual CBT-BN in the adolescent age band (Source: ANZAED CPG Eating disorders 2020; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E) as first-line individual therapy, with the family involved only for meal-time monitoring at home and no formal family therapy sessions across the 20-week treatment protocol
options.rationale: CBT-E is first-line in adults and second-line in adolescents with bulimia if FBT-BN is not indicated or has failed. When family engagement is available, FBT-BN comes first (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

options.text: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) as a stand-alone first-line intervention targeting interpersonal difficulties driving binge-purge cycles, with 16-20 weekly sessions and no direct behavioural work on eating patterns or purging
options.rationale: IPT is a slower-acting alternative to CBT-E in adults with bulimia and is not first-line for adolescents; direct behavioural focus on eating and purge cycles is essential in adolescent presentations (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

options.text: Fluoxetine 60 mg orally daily as first-line monotherapy without psychological therapy, using the recognised anti-bulimic dose to reduce binge and purge frequency across a 12 week trial before any therapy is considered
options.rationale: Fluoxetine 60 mg daily has evidence for adult bulimia but is adjunctive not primary in adolescents; psychological therapy (FBT-BN or CBT-E) is first-line, with SSRI added if inadequate response (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020; AMH).

options.text: Admission to an adolescent inpatient eating-disorder unit for behavioural interruption of the binge-purge cycle under supervised meals, with structured meal exposure and post-meal supervision as the primary treatment modality
options.rationale: Admission for bulimia is reserved for medical instability, failed intensive outpatient care, or acute safety issues; this adolescent is medically stable and treatment-naive (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

explanation.summary: In adolescent bulimia nervosa the Australian first-line psychological therapy is FBT-BN (family-based treatment for bulimia): three phases in which parents initially take charge of eating and interrupt binge-purge cycles, then progressively hand control back to the adolescent. CBT-E is first-line in adults and second-line in adolescents (when family engagement is unavailable or FBT-BN has failed). Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the evidence-based SSRI dose for bulimia but is adjunctive in adolescents. Admission is reserved for medical instability or failed intensive outpatient care.
key_points: Adolescent BN first-line psychological therapy = FBT-BN, not CBT-E
CBT-E is first-line for adults and second-line for adolescents
Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the anti-bulimic dose (adjunctive in adolescents)
Admission is for medical instability or failed intensive outpatient care
Contraindications to FBT: severe trauma, parental psychopathology preventing engagement
explanation.pearls: The FBT phase 1 externalising language (naming the eating disorder as a separate agent) helps parents take charge without turning the adolescent into the problem, mirroring the FBT-AN Maudsley approach. In context: adolescent bulimia therapy choice is family-first when family is available, not individual-first as it is for adults (Source: ANZAED CPG 2020).

subtopic_detail: ADHD - stimulant class choice and formulation for driving
stem:
A 17-year-old boy has been diagnosed with ADHD (combined presentation) after multi-source assessment by a paediatrician, with symptoms since primary school and functional impairment across school and home. Baseline cardiac history and family history for sudden cardiac death are negative, resting ECG is normal, and he has no history of psychosis, substance use disorder, or tics.

He recently obtained his learner driver permit and drives with a supervising parent daily. He needs sustained afternoon concentration for his final school year and part-time evening work, and his previous trial of a short-acting stimulant (2 weeks of dexamphetamine 5 mg twice daily) produced afternoon rebound irritability and inconsistent evening symptom control despite good tolerability during school hours. His parents are engaged in shared decision-making.

data_table.Diagnosis: ADHD combined presentation; multi-source assessment; longstanding impairment
data_table.Cardiac screen: Negative personal + family history; resting ECG within normal limits
data_table.Prior trial: Dexamphetamine 5 mg BD x 2 weeks; afternoon rebound; poor evening cover
data_table.Comorbidity: No psychosis, no SUD, no tics

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological choice?

options.text: Switch to atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily as a non-stimulant first-line agent to avoid any driving impairment risk from stimulants, titrating over 4-6 weeks to a target of 1.2 mg/kg per day for symptom control
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable non-stimulant option but is second-line to stimulants in adolescent ADHD without contraindication; stimulants IMPROVE (not worsen) driving performance in treated ADHD by reducing inattention-related risk (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Continue immediate-release dexamphetamine 5 mg twice daily and add a third afternoon dose of 5 mg at 3 pm to extend cover through evening driving and part-time work, with review of rebound at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Adding a late-afternoon IR dose worsens rebound at the new dose-off time and can impair sleep; a switch to a modified-release formulation is a more coherent solution (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH).

options.text: Switch to methylphenidate osmotic-release 18 mg orally in the morning, titrated fortnightly against symptom control and tolerability, giving 10-12 hours of cover for school, driving and evening work
options.rationale: Switching to a modified-release methylphenidate formulation (osmotic-release, ~10-12 hours) directly addresses both the rebound and the late-day cover issue for a young driver in his final school year with evening work. Modified-release stimulants improve driving performance in treated ADHD compared with untreated ADHD; class-switch from dexamphetamine to methylphenidate is standard when dexamphetamine trial is unsatisfactory (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Withhold pharmacotherapy for the remainder of the driving-permit year and rely on behavioural strategies, executive-function coaching and school accommodations alone until he holds a full unrestricted driver licence
options.rationale: There is no evidence base or Australian guideline recommending stimulant withholding on the basis of a learner permit; treated ADHD lowers crash risk relative to untreated ADHD (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Refer for cardiology review with echocardiogram and Holter monitor as a mandatory pre-requisite before any modified-release stimulant is started in an adolescent with a learner permit and evening work commitments
options.rationale: Routine echo/Holter are not required before adolescent stimulant initiation when personal and family cardiac history are negative and resting ECG is normal; screening is by history and ECG only (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

explanation.summary: Australian first-line pharmacotherapy for adolescent ADHD is a stimulant (methylphenidate or dexamphetamine); non-stimulants (atomoxetine, guanfacine) are second-line. Formulation choice is driven by required duration of cover: IR (~3-4 hours), MR/LA (~8 hours), osmotic-release (~10-12 hours). Class switch (dexamphetamine <-> methylphenidate) is standard when one class fails to control symptoms adequately or produces intolerable rebound. Cardiac screening is by personal and family history plus resting ECG; routine echo or Holter is not indicated when these are negative. Treated ADHD reduces motor-vehicle crash risk relative to untreated ADHD.
key_points: Stimulants are first-line; atomoxetine/guanfacine are second-line
Formulation choice matches required duration of cover
Class-switch between methylphenidate and dexamphetamine is standard next step
Cardiac screening: history + resting ECG (no routine echo/Holter)
Treated ADHD REDUCES crash risk versus untreated ADHD (Austroads)
explanation.pearls: In Australia stimulants are Schedule 8 in most states and require an authority-to-prescribe from a paediatrician, child psychiatrist or (in some states) approved GP with training. In context: adolescent ADHD stimulant selection is a formulation-and-class decision guided by duration of cover, rebound pattern and comorbidity, not a stimulant-versus-nothing decision (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH; Austroads).

subtopic_detail: Late-diagnosis autism spectrum disorder in adolescent girls - masking + comorbid anxiety
stem:
A 15-year-old girl is referred by her GP with 12 months of escalating anxiety, exhaustion after school, selective mutism at school but normal speech at home, and self-reported burn-out after masking her difficulties socially. Her mother describes lifelong subtle social differences (scripted phrases, intense interests in horses and Japanese language, sensory sensitivities to clothing tags and fluorescent light).

She has one long-term female best friend, presents as socially motivated but exhausted, and school reports have historically described her as "quiet but doing well". Two previous CBT courses at headspace addressed anxiety symptoms without lasting benefit. There is no intellectual disability, no history of trauma, and no psychotic features. Vital signs and physical examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Presenting features: 12 months escalating anxiety, post-school exhaustion, selective mutism at school only
data_table.Lifelong features: Scripted phrases, intense narrow interests, sensory sensitivities (tags, fluorescent light)
data_table.Social: One long-term best friend; socially motivated but exhausted from masking
data_table.Prior treatment: Two CBT courses at headspace without lasting benefit
data_table.Investigations: No ID, no trauma history, no psychosis; examination within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in assessment and formulation?

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder with school-refusal features and start sertraline 25 mg orally daily as first-line with weekly review for 4 weeks and a further CBT course focused on social exposure at school
options.rationale: The picture (lifelong scripted phrases, narrow interests, sensory sensitivities, masking-driven exhaustion, home-vs-school speech difference) fits underlying ASD masked in a girl; treating anxiety without formulating ASD misses the driver and prior CBT has already failed (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.text: Formulate as burnout secondary to academic overload and recommend a reduced school-attendance plan, weekly wellness check-ins with the school nurse, and no further mental-health assessment or diagnostic investigation at this stage
options.rationale: Autistic burnout is a recognised concept but the correct pathway is assessment-and-formulation-first, not attendance-reduction without diagnosis; a formal ASD assessment enables appropriate accommodations (Source: Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.text: Diagnose selective mutism as a discrete anxiety disorder and refer for speech pathology and behavioural exposure therapy focused on gradual verbal responses in the school setting with weekly progress monitoring
options.rationale: Selective mutism can be a stand-alone diagnosis in younger children but here it is one facet of a broader ASD-plus-anxiety picture in an adolescent; isolated speech-pathology intervention will not address the underlying formulation (Source: DSM-5-TR; Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.text: Diagnose social anxiety disorder with avoidant features and refer for group-based social skills training with peers, providing psychoeducation to parents about social exposure and homework practice between sessions
options.rationale: Social anxiety does not explain lifelong scripted phrases, narrow intense interests or sensory sensitivities; and generic social skills groups may increase distress in an autistic girl trying to mask (Source: Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

options.text: Refer for a multidisciplinary autism assessment using the Autism CRC national guideline, incorporating a female-presentation-sensitive tool (ADOS-2 module 4 or MIGDAS-2), and formulate anxiety as an ASD comorbidity
options.rationale: The clinical pattern (lifelong scripted phrases, narrow intense interests, sensory sensitivities, masking-driven exhaustion, home-vs-school speech asymmetry) fits ASD masked in a girl. The Autism CRC national guideline (endorsed by NDIS) recommends multidisciplinary assessment with female-sensitive instruments; formulating anxiety as an ASD comorbidity changes therapy targeting to accommodations and anti-masking work (Source: RANZCP FCAP; Autism CRC national guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
Autism CRC national guideline for assessment and diagnosis of autism 2018

explanation.summary: Autism spectrum disorder in adolescent girls is chronically under-recognised because the female phenotype includes social masking, camouflage of stereotypies, one or two close friendships (rather than social isolation), and intense but socially normative interests (horses, animals, celebrities, languages). Presentations often emerge as anxiety, depression, eating disorders or burnout when masking becomes unsustainable in secondary school. The Autism CRC national guideline (endorsed by NDIS since 2018) recommends multidisciplinary assessment using female-sensitive instruments (ADOS-2 module 4 or MIGDAS-2 with clinical formulation). Reframing anxiety as ASD comorbidity changes therapy targets (accommodations, sensory environment, anti-masking, autistic-affirming approaches) rather than repeating standard CBT.
key_points: Girls with ASD often mask, so ASD is missed until secondary school
Female phenotype: 1-2 close friendships, socially normative interests, masking exhaustion
Autism CRC national guideline is the NDIS-endorsed AU standard
Anxiety, depression, eating disorders, burnout are common presenting comorbidities
Standard CBT often fails in autistic girls; autism-adapted CBT or accommodations work better
explanation.pearls: Selective mutism at school but normal speech at home in an adolescent girl is a strong indicator to broaden to an ASD-plus-anxiety formulation rather than treat as isolated selective mutism. In context: adolescent presentations that fail two rounds of standard CBT deserve a neurodevelopmental reformulation, not a third round (Source: Autism CRC national guideline; RANZCP FCAP).
