subtopic_detail: Adolescent suicide - demographic patterns and means-restriction priority
stem:
A 17-year-old boy is brought by his mother to a rural Queensland ED after she found a written suicide note in his room. He has 6 months of low mood after his father's death and 6 weeks of active suicidal ideation with a specific plan to shoot himself with his late father's licensed rifle, currently stored at home in a locked safe. He has recently purchased ammunition online.

He scores 22 on the PHQ-A. Access to alcohol has increased at family gatherings since the bereavement. He denies psychosis and has no prior suicide attempts. He has agreed to admission today. On formal assessment there is active intent, a specific plan with available means, no protective factors mitigating the plan, and a recent behavioural rehearsal step. His mother is present, distressed, but supportive and willing to act on any plan you make.

data_table.Bereavement: Father died 6 months ago; escalating family alcohol use
data_table.Suicidality: 6 weeks active ideation, specific plan (firearm), means available (rifle in home safe), recent ammunition purchase
data_table.Risk factors: Male, rural, firearm access, bereavement, alcohol
data_table.Consent: Agreed to admission; mother present and willing to act

lead_in: In addition to psychiatric admission for stabilisation, what is the single highest-priority intervention today?

options.text: Arrange immediate removal of the firearm and ammunition from the home today with the mother's consent, coordinated with Queensland Police weapons licensing to secure the rifle off-site before any discharge is considered
options.rationale: Means restriction is the single highest-evidence-per-hour intervention in suicide prevention. Firearms have a case-fatality ratio near 85 percent versus <5 percent for most other methods, so removing the specific planned lethal means from the home substantially reduces short-term risk even if ideation persists. Australian firearm law permits removal via licensed transfer or police storage (Source: Black Dog Institute means-restriction guidance; Queensland Police weapons licensing; Beyond Blue).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 10 mg orally daily today with 1 week review for tolerability and emergent suicidality per the black-box warning, alongside psychology follow-up within 72 hours of discharge from the admission
options.rationale: SSRI initiation is reasonable but is not the single highest-yield intervention TODAY because SSRI effect takes weeks to onset and does not address the immediate lethal-means-in-home issue that drives short-term risk (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic; ANZCTR firearm means restriction evidence).

options.text: Complete a structured suicide-risk assessment tool such as the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale to categorise him as high risk and use the numerical score to determine level of observation and length of admission stay
options.rationale: Structured risk stratification tools have poor positive predictive value for suicide and should not be used to determine level of care in isolation; they do not replace means restriction as the highest-yield acute intervention (Source: RANZCP; NICE NG225 Self-harm).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
NICE NG225 Self-harm assessment and management

options.text: Have him sign a written no-suicide contract with explicit undertakings not to act on suicidal thoughts for 30 days as a discharge criterion, with copies retained in his medical record and provided to his mother
options.rationale: No-suicide contracts have no evidence for reducing suicide risk and can create false clinician reassurance; they have been superseded by collaborative safety planning (Source: Stanley-Brown SPI; RANZCP FCAP).
source_refs: RANZCP Faculty of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry

options.text: Restrict his access to social media and internet platforms for the first two weeks post-discharge to reduce exposure to potentially triggering content, coordinated by his mother with parental-control filters on all his devices
options.rationale: Blanket social-media restriction is not evidence-based first-line and does not address the specific in-home firearm plan; targeted safe-messaging discussions may complement care but do not substitute for means restriction (Source: headspace CPG; Mindframe).

explanation.summary: In Australian youth suicide the male-to-female ratio for completion is approximately 3:1, rural rates exceed urban rates, and firearms account for a disproportionately high case-fatality ratio in rural presentations. Means restriction has the strongest single-intervention evidence for reducing suicide mortality. When a plan is specific and the means are in the home, restricting access to that specific method saves lives even when substitution to other methods is possible, because most attempts are ambivalent, impulsive at the moment of action, and the transition between one method and another is not automatic. Structured risk tools (C-SSRS, SAD PERSONS) have poor predictive validity for individual suicide; no-suicide contracts are not evidence-based; collaborative safety planning has replaced both.
key_points: Means restriction is the highest-evidence suicide-prevention intervention
Firearms: case-fatality ~85% vs <5% for many other methods
AU rural youth suicide rate > urban; male:female completion ~3:1
Structured risk tools have poor PPV; do not replace clinical formulation
No-suicide contracts are superseded by collaborative safety planning
explanation.pearls: Under Queensland weapons legislation a family member or police can remove a firearm from a licensed owner's home when there is a mental health concern, without requiring the licence-holder's consent for temporary safe storage. In context: adolescent suicide-risk management is means-first, medication-second, therapy-third within the first 24 hours (Source: Black Dog Institute; QPS weapons licensing).

subtopic_detail: Early psychosis - ultra-high-risk criteria and EPPIC referral
stem:
A 16-year-old girl is reviewed at headspace with 8 weeks of a new belief that her classmates are subtly whispering about her when she walks past; she recognises the belief may not be true and finds it distressing. She has withdrawn socially, marks have dropped, and she now scores in the borderline range on the SOFAS with a 30-point drop from her prior baseline over 12 months.

Her mother has a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder. She has no positive family history of any other psychiatric condition, no substance use on collateral, and no head injury. There are no frank hallucinations, no clear delusions held with full conviction, and no formal thought disorder. Vital signs and neurological examination are within normal limits. Basic metabolic and thyroid screens are within normal limits.

data_table.Attenuated psychotic symptoms: 8 weeks of paranoid ideation with retained insight; distressing; subthreshold conviction
data_table.Function: SOFAS in borderline range; 30-point drop over 12 months
data_table.Substance and neurological: No substance use on collateral; no head injury; neurological examination within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Metabolic and thyroid screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 1 mg orally daily today as first-line pharmacological intervention on the basis of a first-degree family history plus attenuated psychotic symptoms with functional decline in the ultra-high-risk pattern
options.rationale: Australian EIS/EPPIC guidance does NOT recommend antipsychotic initiation for ultra-high-risk presentations without frank psychosis; the evidence for prophylactic antipsychotic is weak, side-effect burden is significant, and most UHR individuals do not transition (Source: EPPIC EIS clinical practice guidance; Orygen youth mental health guidance).

options.text: Refer to the early intervention psychosis service (or equivalent local EIS) for structured ultra-high-risk assessment and CAARMS interview, and offer evidence-based CBT for UHR states while monitoring for frank transition
options.rationale: She meets the ultra-high-risk (UHR / clinical high-risk) pattern via attenuated psychotic symptoms plus genetic risk with functional decline. Australian EIS/EPPIC (Orygen) guidance recommends specialist EIS assessment with the CAARMS (Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States), and offers CBT for UHR with active monitoring rather than antipsychotic initiation. Approximately 15-25 percent of UHR individuals transition to a first psychotic episode within 2-3 years (Source: EPPIC EIS; Orygen; CAARMS).
source_refs: CAARMS Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States

options.text: Diagnose brief psychotic disorder based on 8 weeks of persecutory beliefs with functional decline in an adolescent, and arrange same-day acute inpatient adolescent mental-health admission for observation and diagnostic clarification
options.rationale: She has retained insight, subthreshold conviction, no hallucinations, and no formal thought disorder - she does not meet brief psychotic disorder criteria, which require frank psychosis (Source: DSM-5-TR; EPPIC EIS clinical practice guidance).

options.text: Formulate this as social anxiety disorder with paranoid features driven by peer-comparison stress, and refer for group-based social-skills training combined with GP-delivered supportive counselling and school liaison over 6 weeks
options.rationale: Social anxiety does not explain a 30-point SOFAS decline over 12 months in an adolescent with a first-degree relative with schizoaffective disorder; the pattern warrants formal UHR assessment, not reformulation as social anxiety (Source: EPPIC EIS; DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Discharge from headspace to primary-care GP follow-up in 3 months given retained insight and absence of frank psychosis, with GP-led escalation only if new hallucinations or delusions with full conviction subsequently develop
options.rationale: UHR is the highest-yield window for early intervention; discharge to routine review loses the opportunity to reduce transition risk with CBT and active monitoring (Source: EPPIC EIS; Orygen).

explanation.summary: Ultra-high-risk (UHR) for psychosis, also called clinical high-risk, is assessed by CAARMS or SIPS and encompasses three overlapping pathways: attenuated psychotic symptoms (retained insight, subthreshold conviction/frequency/duration), brief limited intermittent psychotic symptoms (BLIPS - frank but brief and self-limited), and genetic risk plus deterioration (first-degree family history plus functional decline). Australian EPPIC / EIS guidance (Orygen) recommends specialist assessment, CBT for UHR states with active monitoring, and NO prophylactic antipsychotic; roughly 15-25 percent of UHR individuals transition to a first psychotic episode over 2-3 years, so most benefit from psychological intervention alone.
key_points: 3 UHR pathways: attenuated symptoms, BLIPS, genetic risk + deterioration
CAARMS or SIPS structured interview is the assessment tool
Australian EIS/EPPIC offers CBT for UHR + monitoring, NOT prophylactic antipsychotic
~15-25% transition to frank psychosis over 2-3 years
Antipsychotics reserved for frank psychosis, not attenuated symptoms
explanation.pearls: The Orygen EPPIC model provides youth-specific psychosis care (12-25 years) with an initial 5-year specialised service window because outcome trajectory is most modifiable in this period. In context: adolescent early-psychosis pathways are graded (UHR - first episode - established), and antipsychotic initiation aligns to frank psychosis not to at-risk states (Source: EPPIC; Orygen).

sources.label: CAARMS Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States

subtopic_detail: Adolescent bipolar recognition and mood-stabiliser selection
stem:
A 17-year-old girl is reviewed 4 weeks after being started on fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily for what her GP diagnosed as major depressive disorder. Since starting she has slept 3 hours per night, become elated with pressured speech, spent her entire term-time savings on online purchases in one afternoon, and had unprotected sex with two new partners in the past week.

Collateral from her mother identifies a maternal aunt with lithium-treated bipolar I disorder. Reviewing history reveals a self-limited 4-day episode of decreased sleep, increased energy and impulsive spending at age 15 that resolved spontaneously and was not disclosed at the original assessment. Vital signs are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is negative and TSH, LFTs and calcium are within normal limits.

data_table.Presenting episode: 4 weeks post-fluoxetine start: sleep 3 h, elated, pressured speech, hypersexuality, impulsive spending
data_table.Prior episode (age 15): 4 days decreased sleep + increased energy + impulsivity, self-limited, not previously disclosed
data_table.Family history: Maternal aunt with lithium-treated bipolar I
data_table.Substances and metabolic: UDS negative; TSH, LFTs, corrected Ca within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Continue fluoxetine at the current dose, add quetiapine 25 mg orally at night as an adjunct for agitation and impaired sleep, and review the working diagnosis of major depression with mixed features at 2 weeks
options.rationale: Continuing an antidepressant during a stimulant-emergent mania perpetuates the destabilising exposure; the DSM-5 antidepressant-induced-mania criterion re-classifies this as bipolar disorder (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood disorders; TG Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline: Mood disorders

options.text: Cease fluoxetine and commence lamotrigine 25 mg orally daily as first-line mood stabiliser to cover bipolar depression prophylaxis, titrating slowly over 6 weeks to reduce risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has better evidence for bipolar depression and maintenance than for acute mania; the current picture is acute mania precipitated by SSRI and needs an anti-manic agent (lithium, quetiapine or valproate). Lamotrigine's slow titration also makes it unsuitable for acute mania (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood disorders; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline: Mood disorders

options.text: Cease fluoxetine and commence sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily as first-line mood stabiliser for acute mania, provide contraception counselling, and arrange fortnightly LFT and drug-level review
options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated as first-line in women of childbearing potential unless a pregnancy-prevention program is in place and other options are exhausted, because of major teratogenicity (neural tube defects, foetal valproate syndrome, cognitive impairment); TGA has strengthened warnings (Source: TGA valproate safety update; AMH; RANZCP CPG).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline: Mood disorders

options.text: Cease fluoxetine, admit for stabilisation, and start lithium as first-line mood stabiliser for acute mania given the family lithium-response predictor, targeting a serum level 0.8-1.0 mmol/L after baseline workup
options.rationale: The picture is antidepressant-induced mania meeting DSM-5 bipolar I criteria (retrospective 4-day hypomanic episode at 15 supports intrinsic bipolarity). Lithium is the first-line mood stabiliser in adolescent bipolar I with a strongly positive family lithium-response history, per RANZCP CPG. Pre-treatment workup covers renal, thyroid, parathyroid, ECG and pregnancy; target serum level 0.8-1.0 mmol/L in acute mania (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood disorders; TG Psychotropic; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline: Mood disorders

options.text: Cease fluoxetine and initiate olanzapine 10 mg orally daily as first-line acute-mania monotherapy, arrange baseline weight and metabolic screen, and review at 2 weeks with a plan to add lithium if response is inadequate
options.rationale: Olanzapine is an option in acute mania but is disfavoured first-line in an adolescent because of the substantial metabolic burden (weight gain, dyslipidaemia); when family history predicts lithium response, lithium is preferred (Source: RANZCP CPG; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline: Mood disorders

explanation.summary: SSRI-emergent mania in a young person meets DSM-5 bipolar I criteria and re-classifies the underlying diagnosis. First-line pharmacological management is (a) cease the antidepressant and (b) start an anti-manic mood stabiliser: lithium, quetiapine, olanzapine or valproate. In an adolescent female of childbearing potential, valproate is avoided unless a pregnancy-prevention program is in place (TGA teratogenicity warning). Lithium is first-line in bipolar I with a strong family history of lithium response and requires pre-treatment renal, thyroid, parathyroid, calcium, ECG and pregnancy screen; target serum level 0.6-1.0 mmol/L (0.8-1.0 in acute mania). Lamotrigine is best in bipolar depression and maintenance, not acute mania.
key_points: SSRI-emergent mania = bipolar I diagnosis (DSM-5)
First step: cease the antidepressant AND start an anti-manic agent
Lithium first-line when family lithium-response predicts benefit
Valproate contraindicated first-line in females of childbearing potential
Lamotrigine is for bipolar depression / maintenance, not acute mania
explanation.pearls: Retrospective mining for a self-limited hypomanic episode is the single most useful clarifying step whenever a young patient develops apparent SSRI-emergent mania; often a 3-4 day episode at age 14-16 was dismissed by family as "a phase". In context: adolescent bipolar recognition changes both diagnosis and treatment axis, and any SSRI initiation without a bipolar screen risks precipitating exactly this presentation (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood disorders; TG Psychotropic; TGA valproate warning).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline: Mood disorders
